title: Mr. and Mrs. A.C. Synigal Interview, 1962-05-24

blocks.x: Let's see, this is a real one of an interview. We're making it at 1938, is that right? 1938 Laferroose Street, and today is May the 20-something. 24th. May the 24th, 19...
It's Thursday, May the 24th.
1962. Let's get your names on here again.
This is Alphonse C. Senegal.
And you?

Edna B. Senegal. Wait, I want my full name. This is Edna Bibelet Serena Senegal. That's my children's name, Serena. And I tell them about this tape. And Mother, you didn't put our name on there. You put an S. And it's Serena. Serena is the Spanish part of our family. So we should have Serena. This is my second marriage in Senegal. Our first marriage was to Serena. And he was the one that his grandfather came from Spain. So it's my children's grandfather. Great grandfather, see. And, uh, of course, French, came from my father. He's a peopleist. And my mother, I didn't say my mother's name, was Marceline LeBlanc. And I'm a mother. LeBlanc. Would you like Marceline? That's a pretty name. That's a beautiful name. Yeah, Marceline LeBlanc. That is my mother's name. Yeah. And, and... Okay, Marjorie Zander.
And I'm Dick Allen. I want to put our own names on here so that everybody will know what's what. Who's who. Who's who's going on. Who's who.
And, um, I want to say this. My, my famous grandmother, who I take after, was Suzanne. That's French. S-A-Z, how do you spell Suzanne? S-A-S-U-Z-A-N-E. S-U-Z-A-N-E.
That's right.

Suzanne. She doesn't like Susan. But her name was Suzanne LeBlanc. And she was a grand old lady of the whole family. She had this big plantation home that her husband died in her four-post bed. And he was a white man. He was a pure white man. You want me to tell? Sure. You want me to tell her why? She was a nurse. And so she took care of his face with, um, I think he had four boys. One just recently died out there in, uh, Ascension Parish. I'm sorry I didn't get to see him. Because he asked for me. One, not me, he didn't know me. But he asked of one of Johnny Beboleyn's children. And, uh, so I was the only one left. And my uncle out there, he said, why didn't I go to see him? Because he was a very rich man. Perhaps he would have gave me something. So, uh, this man was, um, what's my grandfather's name? Uh, Bebole?
Uh, LeBlanc.
The old man, my sister took the old man's picture. Oh yeah, LeBlanc. Huh? Huh?
No. Johnny LeBlanc?
No, Johnny Bebole was my, my father. But, uh, the old man LeBlanc that died in my grand, my grandmother's bed. Oh yeah. Uh, hmm.
The old man's picture.

Those old people, they come and they go. The names come and go. But anyway, he was an old Frenchman. And my grandmother was a nurse. She spoke French. His wife had cancer. And he called her in to take care of his wife and his children. We had four children. And she died. My grandmother still stayed there and took care of the children, boys, the four daughters. They adored my grandmother. They did everything for her. Everything. One of them was a lawyer. The other two were something. But anyway, they took care of her until she died. And so, they had this beautiful plantation. Not the, not the house that he lived in. But this house that he gave my grandmother is out there now. We go, I take my children out there to see it all the time. They're still standing. And, um, I showed them the room that my grandmother lived in. And then, my mother and my grandfather died in. And, you know, it's very big four-poster bed. Have you ever seen them? Yeah. Hi, hi, baby. You can step up on a step to get in. Well, that's the bed like that he died in. And so, he left word when he died to his son to always take care of her because she was so good to their mother. And until they died, they took care of her. She was such a sweet old lady. All the people in the countryside in those days, they didn't have no automobiles at all. They had these, uh, carriages. Now, you see these carriages that we rode in the other day? That wasn't new to me. I rode in those that go to school. To go to school. Because we went to school, uh, we live in a mile and a half from Donaldsonville. In this great big plantation home. We had the largest home out there. And if you have a chance to make a trip out there, I can tell you where this home is and you can see it. It's well kept, beautiful, and the people will let you go in there. If you just say the Bibeles, uh, uh, wants to someone from the Bibeles family want to see the home. So, uh, it's really, and it's well kept up until this very day. While all the other places are gone, that's still standing. So, uh, um, my mother, after my grandmother died in that home, my mother lived there. She raised her family there with my father. My father died first. My father died there in that home. And then we came to New Orleans because my mother was a dressmaker from Odise. And she sold for the Bartons. You know of the Bartons? They're very, very rich plantation homes out there in Ascension or Assumption Parish. Their home is out there. On that road, on that new road. The Bartons, they, they're, oh, well known. Oh, it should be in history.
I know some Bartons, but I don't know if they are the same kind.

Oh, I imagine they must be the same. They have the, that plantation home where the big posts go all the way up to the second porch, you know. From the first porch, the big columns goes up. And my mother sold for them. And, uh, most of the rich people out there, uh, when my father was living here, he was a butcher. And, um, he, uh, he sold his meat to, um, most of the rich people out there. He used to go out in these wagons. I don't know if you know, you're too young to know that. Well, anyhow, he had a wagon. I was the oldest child. My mother and father had seven children. I was the oldest. And he had this bell. I had the bell. I had the bell. Did you get the bell out?
Yeah, those bells were a cowbell. Yeah. It's like a cowbell.
It's like the rag band rings right here.
Ring the bell.

And the people would come out to buy the meat. You see? And so, um, uh, what do I want to say about this? So I kept this bell all these many years. And every new year, we get this bell out and ring. Go all around the house, ring this bell. So this year, he was in California for New Year's. So my little granddaughter was here and my grandson. And oh, they all pushed each other. Where is the bell? Where is the bell? Let me ring the bell. And so finally, we have two bells. I think they found the other, but they couldn't find. First year that we didn't ring the bell for New Year's was this year because he wasn't here. He was in California. So, and then we moved from after my father died. My mother, um, she said she couldn't make a living out there with those seven children. So she came here. She could do better here. She had an aunt here. She lived not far from here. On Rushblaive and, uh, Rushblaive and Ton- Rushblaive and what? No, no, no. Rushblaive right out here somewhere. And, uh, she used to visit her. So she said, why don't you come to New Orleans? You could do better with that beautiful sewing you do than out there with the few rich people you couldn't do well. So we sewed out everything. Now my father, he had men, we had, uh, how many acres? What was that? How many acres of land we had? I said 27 acres. The old man told us when we went out there last summer how many acres. I believe he said 27 acres. Oh, man. Oh, honey. It was all the way back to the river, all the way back to the river and to the canal. It's about 80 acres of land we had all that. And so my father used to lease it out to men to grow things on it, you see? And they had, that year they had pumpkins. They had everything. And the pumpkins was all over the sheds in the yard and all. After my father died, here was all the pumpkins. And my mother had this race horse. I'll never forget. Diamond they called him. Name was Diamond. And my mother used to drive this, uh, you see when you, uh, we lived a mile and a half from Donathanville. And about 10 miles, is it 10 miles to Thibodeau? Uh, 10 miles. And we used to go to Mass. We used to go to Mass in Thibodeau sometimes. It wasn't that far though.
From where you all went to? To Thibodeau, you remember?

We, uh, well right out to Thibodeau. We'd go, my mother would drive us when I was a little girl, about 10 years old. We used to go to Thibodeau to Mass. And that's about 10 miles or something. Well, she'd have this horse on her. Well, it wasn't a, it wasn't a surrey. It was a buggy. Do you know what a buggy is? It was a buggy. Was she a buggy? No. Uh, she would, um, it was a buggy. My sister and I would have, uh, we'd sit on side when she, she'd have those, and it was, he was a race horse, this Diamond. My father had him as a race horse. And so she began to drive him. And used to drive him on Sunday morning, drive us to church. And here we were sitting on the side of her. And our curls, lulled curls would be just flying out. My mother would be holding, I can remember how she'd be holding the race horse, you know. And we'd get there in no time, uh, for these, uh, with this, with this race horse. Nobody couldn't drive him but my mother. And we used to go to church on Sunday morning. And go to, we used to go to school. We had one of those carriages, surrey's there, with the fringe on it. We used to go to school in that. Um, to Donisonville. That was a mile and a half.
Which direction is the plantation home from? Donisonville?
Um, going towards, Tibidon.

That's all, that's all, that's out from Tibidon. A mile and a half? Yeah. That's a, for instance, you cross the U.P. Long Bridge, you know. Oh yeah. And get that, keep you all the way going to Tibidon. And you wouldn't turn left, continue right. On the bayou.

Yeah, on the bayou. On the bayou. On that bayou. Bayou Lafour. On that road. On that road. Continue on that bayou Lafour. A mile and a half from Donisonville. Donisonville. On bayou Lafour. And you can't miss it because that great big Catholic church is there. Noted, oh, it's been there over a hundred years. Since, what, St. uh, the Ascension. The Ascension. The Ascension. The Catholic church. There where I was christened there. And, uh, made my communion there. That big church. And in those days, now, I don't want to talk politics and anything like that. But in those days, we had no segregation. I made my communion. Thanks to white girls. Well, it's far different in those days from these days. I was at the Holy Family. I came to the Holy Family Convent here during my retreat. Because one of the sisters from out there came. And he used to take us, everybody brought me here. And then that Saturday evening, we went back home. And made my communion that Sunday morning. And, um, I, when my children, when I take my children out there, I show them the seat I was sitting in. And don't you know they know it when we go now, the smallest one. This is where my mayor used to sit when she made her communion. And they handed it all the way down. Everybody knows it now. So, uh, and well, those are nice things to remember, you know. And, uh, I remember when there's no segregation at all. I know you all, you don't remember. Of course, you were too young. I'm sure both of you. But when I was a little girl, about ten years old, Tim, we lived in the country and I came here. We used to come off first. We came here often. And, uh, I remember, um, wait, we moved here. When we moved here, we moved on a boat. Now, I can't, that's one thing I can't remember, is the boat we moved on. Remember they had those boats coming back and forth? We moved here on a boat. Now, I can't remember which boat. If they called the names of the boat, maybe I could remember that. So, we had to get the Espinade. We got down on Espinade Wharf. Espinade and the river. We got down on the bus. And we got the Espinade car. I know whether the wagon or truck or something took the furniture. But we got on the street car. There was no buses then. Got on the street car and that's one thing I can remember as a child. Well, my brothers and sisters, they hardly came, but I would always come with my aunt and everything. And I got in the street car and ran all the way to the front seat. All the way to the front seat. Now, I can remember it just as plain as today. And I was a child then. So, when I tell that to people, they said, older people than me, they said, well, you're telling the truth. There was no segregation there. There really was no segregation there. That's what I heard. It was the truth. It was the truth. I did it. I know. That's one thing I remember doing myself. And I told them, I said, I'm sure I'm not imagining that. I said, I did that. I said, yes, you did. I asked the old people about it. And they said, sure, there was no segregation there. It's just recently in about, how many years? About 30? Less than?
More than 30 years?
Oh, yeah.
Since about, around 1910.
You think that's how old? Oh, yeah.
So, they were good.
Probably back from 1900. I didn't remember.
So, anyway.

And things were going on just as nice and nobody. My mother came in here and we lived on Priya. Priya, the Wogan's. You know where the Wogan's live? On Priya and Espinade? Those are very old, rich people. On Espinade and Priya. And my mother came here and I don't know how it came with the neighbors and all. They told the Wogan's that my mother was a modi. So, she starts running right away. Being a neighbor, she went to see. Then they sent it to different ones and all. Then I was 14 when my father died. We moved here and I began sewing with her. And I sewed with her practically until she died. I'm making all those beautiful queen maid's costumes and made good money. See, she came right in here. Of course, good money in those days. But my, I, as we went on, and then for years and years I sewed with my mother until I married my first husband. He was Victor Serena. And, well, I didn't sew while I was mad. I just did a little to help her because I began having children. I had four children for him. And so, of course, I had to keep house and take care of him. But I would help her when she'd get too much work. You know, I'd go around and help her. So, but my husband had a terrible accident. His death, he was drowned. He was drowned and, and, of course, that's what's so sad. Just broke up my home life. I went to live with my mother. And then I began sewing. Really had to sew then to help my children and my mother. She was a widow. My mother was a widow, so we were together. And I stayed eight years a widow when he came along. When he came along. That was the end of eight years. That was the end of eight years. And he was a widow three years, huh? Your wife was dead three years. And we brought the family together. He had three or four children. I had three. Three children.
He had four.

And I had four. And you can buy them. And they'd sell them. And, oh, everybody was talking. I said, how are you all going to do that? Big family, get it together. And he was an insurance man then, making good money. And I was making good money. So, when only, we made it. I said, like a lady, a friend of mine, she's married a second time. And her husband has one little girl, 14 years old. So, she came here crying on my shoulder. Oh, I made a terrible mistake. I said, what do you mean? What do you mean? She says, oh, I don't know. I made a terrible mistake. That little girl is about to send me crazy. 14 years old. She's about to send me crazy. I said, what? Send me crazy? Well, suppose you had seven, huh? Four and three. Seven like I did. I said, suppose you'd have seven like I did. And then had to work too. I said, of course you had to. She's an Avon. She's an Avon specialist. She's the head of all Avons in New Orleans. And a wonderful job like you have. And worried about one little girl. She said, but that little girl is not anybody crazy. I said, she wouldn't send me crazy. Because I let her know who is boss. So, she said, I tried to do that. But he just spoiled me. You know, that's his only child. He just spoiled her. I said, well, spoil him and spoil her too. But let them know when it's time, you know, to be. So, finally, she went home and she said, I did what you said, Ms. Sengal. I said, well, what happened? Everything is okidokid. I let them know I was boss. I said, well, that's what you had to do. So, everything is going on nicely. So, um.
Well, what kind of music did you hear in Donaldsonville when you were growing up? Did they have dances there? Or?

Billika Sand. Did you hear Billika Sand? Sure. He used to come in. I went to the sisters of the Holy Family. She paid to him. Holy Family School out there. Holy Family Sisters from here. They had a school and that's where I went to school. And he used to give concerts for the sisters out there. Billika Sand. And who else used to come out there? Well, that was a main feature.
That was a main feature of him.
Oh, and Billika Sand would come out there. The whole countryside would go.
And he'd open his mouth.

He'd open his mouth so wide. Open his mouth so wide. All the children would try to imitate him. And of course, the Holy Family Sisters always gave nice concerts. I used to bring practically all of them. All of the, all of the concerts. They always gave nice concerts. And, um, who else? I can't, I can't remember.
They said what kind of music did you all play? You know, you used to play music. She played piano.

Yeah, I played piano. Oh, well, Claude Williams. Didn't you ask me about Claude Williams? Yeah. Well, Claude Williams, you know, he originated from that. He was born in Donisonville. And his son is playing now, I think, in Baton Rouge. And he has a daughter who is a nun. I think she's still a nun. And he was my mother's groomsman when she got married. So we were intimate. We were close friends. His daughter is here in the world?
I think she's in the country on all these streets. The Holy Family is going.
I think she's in the mother house. She might be in the mother house.
And you can get touched with her, huh?

I played with Claude Williams. I was taking music with, who did I start taking music with? I started taking music out there, I believe, with one of the sisters. The Holy Family sisters. There were nuns out there as a child. And when I came over here, I lived next door to a white lady who was giving lessons. The lady lived between us and the Wogan's. The Wogan's on the corner. And so I take lessons from her. And, well, I could play very well. I could play all kinds of music, but it was mostly sentimental music, I think. Like on Sunday afternoon, you would think we'd have a party, how we'd congregate together and sing and play the piano. That was the only music we had in those days. That was only the boys we picked on. It was piano playing. Canna playing.
They didn't have those shows like they have now.

No, no picture shows, no. No picture shows. No picture shows. They didn't have no picture shows. They didn't have victroles and nothing like that. They just were beginning to have these photographs. The big horns, the big horns.
The earphones.

Yeah, they came out first with the earphones. You'd have to be listening to it. You couldn't hear it. You had to have these earphones to listen to. And I tell you what I do. The shows had still music.
They didn't have any music with it. The place that the show had still music. They have to play music.

Well, now that's about all the music I know from there. But I tell you, I have something. I have a sheet music that my daughter composed. But I wouldn't want her, I wouldn't want you to write to her. And involve her in it. Well, you could hear her. No, no, it made her sick the last time. You see, she has seven books. She lives in Richmond, Virginia. She was one time a nun. She was a nun for four years in the convent. And she, well, they give you six years to make up your mind. Every year they give you. And you can sign or not sign. So, oh, I thought, sure. And then she had gone to Rock Castle in Virginia at school. You know her at school? Color school, Rock Castle, Virginia. Girls only. Well, she had a scholarship and she went there. And so when she came back, oh, I thought, sure, she was going to teach her something. Because, oh, had this priest here at Corpus Christi. Corpus Christi had a job waiting for her to teach. And had so many plans and everything. She had wrote several times, jokingly, that she was going to wear a veil. Mother, you'd be surprised if you see me wearing a veil when I come home. You know, that way. And I wouldn't. I said, oh, she's just joking. She's not. So finally when she came home, I said, Melda, what are you going to do? She finished, graduated, you know. She said, Imelda, what's her name? Imelda Sarendra. She says, I don't know. She says, I think I'm going to the convent. She says, I can't then. She says, yes, Mother, I think I'm going. I said, well, you know, it's up to you. But all those years of study and all that. And I said, then you're in the convent. She said, well, they need teachers. They need teachers in the convent. They need smart. They don't need only scrub women in the convent. They need people like me to help them out. I says, but not you. I said, they need people like you, but not you. Oh, she says, yes, Mother, they do. Don't feel like that. And so I said, well, not going to say far again. So she just went on. She stole away one day and went to the convent. And so she stayed in there four years and came out. Now I was so satisfied to have her in there then. I made up her mind, you know. But then she came out and had seven boys. Imagine, came out and had seven boys. And wonderful, seven wonderful boys. Wonderful. All kinds of ways. Two of them in there. Two are in there. Two are in there. She must have had a love. All boys, not even a girl. Every time she said, Mother, this is going to be a girl. I just know it. I just know it. Come a boy. And so she just wrote me a letter yesterday. I got this letter. Say, Mother, try to come over in June. The boys are going to be here. And let's make it more merry. You and part Senegal come over and we'll have a house full. And we'll have a merry time. So, to get in now, get back to this. After she got out of the town, then she started having children. I guess too close together. They were about a year apart. And she got nervous. She was terribly nervous. So nervous that I had her husband. But she had a wonderful family. His family. And he was a wonderful man to her. He still is. And an old lady was an Indian type of old lady. She was half Indian. As I say, this mixture. But she had more Indian blood in her than anything else. And she was just wonderful to her. She said, Ms. Senegal, don't worry. When you're gone, I'm her mother. And, well, she took this nervous breakdown. They had to send for me. I went over there and got her and brought her here. And I brought her to, I had, by sewing, I knew so many rich white people that could help me. And they knew this, uh, doctor, uh, Hotel Dieu, that famous doctor, metal doctor, Hotel Dieu. Oh, yes, indeed. They brought me, um, the noise even had her going there just with all the people. No segregation. You know, they said, you bring Melda in there and just say, we sent her there. And so we were treated just like anybody else. And he just took, oh, he just took so much patience with her. And when I told him about the children, oh, he said, what a pity a beautiful woman like that. And all these boys to live for her. And, um, and the thing of it, she didn't think she was nervous. And she didn't look nervous. And to look at her, you wouldn't think she was nervous. But it was inside. That's what the doctor said, it was inward, you know. And she was holding it all in. Smart. Oh, she was smart as she can be. So finally the doctor told her, he said, um, he says, well, you're nervous, my dear child. He says, no doctor, I am not nervous. He says, yes, you are nervous. He says, yes, you are nervous. I said, well, how can you tell? He says, I can tell. He said, can you tell me why I'm nervous or how? He says, because you are nervous. He told the nurse to go get a glass of water. And he says, now, if you can hold that glass of water still, as I do, then you'll know you're nervous. I said, oh, you're nervous. All right. She said, all right. You got to get a glass of water. So she says, you hold it first. I said, you hold it. Oh, I said, oh, Mel is shaking my goodness. Tell the doctor what to do. And so he held the water and he was holding it and it was shaking, you know, just shaking a little bit. She says, now, doctor, can't you see it shaking? He says, oh, no, I'm just a little upset. He said, but it's not shaking. I'm a little upset. But he said, she said, doctor, but you see it shaking, don't you? He said, a little upset, that's all. I said, now you do it. She took the place and held it up. Just as still, not even a quiver. So she said, now, who is nervous? You are. I mean, it was something. So he said, well, all right, we compromise on that. You just come see me a couple of times. We'll find out who's nervous. I'm nervous or you're nervous. So to get back to this, she had this nervous breakdown. And during her sickness, she wrote the most beautiful poems. I'm going to get this to show you now. But I don't want it to, I don't want you to write to her about it. Because I don't want it to go back, you know, into that nervous state, you know.
You ought to get our music too.
You're not nervous because she wrote all that. Yeah. Well, we've got about a second left.
How old was Bunk Johnson, did you say?

Well, Bunk Johnson was, let me see, when Bunk Johnson died, I think Bunk Johnson was about 60 to 80 years old, close to 70, at that time. So he's older than you, huh? He's older than I, yeah. He's about four or five years old. Bunk Johnson was a fine, good age, fine man. She wrote there.

And a record, a record she wrote, a wonderful record she wrote. She wrote to D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&D for D&
As I say, not because she's my daughter. She's smart. I've heard so many people say how smart she was.

Let me put, this is real too, and we're interviewing Mr. and Mrs. AC Senegal. It's May the 24th, 1962 Thursday. And I'm looking at this piece of sheet music. I see it's copyrighted 1924. That's right. Is that right? And it's got a picture of your daughter. Imelda Serena Robinson. And the music is by J. Charles McNeil. Is that a local McNeil? No, he's from, I think he's from California. He must have been a very talented lady to write this. And they recorded some of her, one of her songs. Was this song they recorded? No, no, no. He recorded another song that he was singing.

I'm going to look at that record. I have a record here. And she was dying over. But her husband said, oh, Mrs. Senegal, don't rush her. Don't push her with this. Because I need her with these children. More than that, you know? So I, you know, she'd write to me. And mother, do this, write to the, I wouldn't. I said, no. She was, needed more at home with her children than this town. Yeah. But if she had tech on. Now she wrote to New York. And New York, her company wanted to take her, take her poems, you know, her writings, you know, and all. So then I'd tell her, I'd say, oh, don't do that now. I'd say, your home life is needed more. After she had gotten nervous, well then, you know, her home, home life was needed more than all that. So. You know, I'll look up that record someday and see. See for, oh, it's a beautiful piece of music. Now that's about all that. That's about all I've learned.
Well, I wanted to ask you about Billy Kersan. How did he happen to come to Donaldson's then?
Where, where was he from? I don't know.
I think Billy Kersan came from Donaldson then. Did he?
Yeah.
I heard that. He did? Yeah. Billy Kersan came from Donaldson. Billy Kersan used to ride those steamboats. They had, they had shows on those. What you used to call those shows again?
Night shows. I mean, showboats.

Showboats. Showboats. Showboats. They used to travel from one bayou, one section to another. I remember when Bill Kersan came to New Iberia on a showboat.
